lead.eyebrow: Islamabad MOU Is Dead in All But Name — Trump Declares Ceasefire "Over"; US Strikes Kharg Island; Seizure Threat Targets 90% of Iran's Crude Exports; Brent Holds Near $77 as Markets Price the Worst
lead.headline: Trump Says Ceasefire Is "Over" After US Strikes Kharg Island — IRGC Retaliates Against 85 US Bases; Kharg Seizure Would Remove 2.5–3 mb/d From Global Supply; Brent Surged 5%+ Wednesday, Holds $76.57 Friday
paragraphs: Three weeks after the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was signed on June 17, the ceasefire it codified is effectively dead. Speaking from the NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, President Trump declared: "I think it's over. I don't want to deal with them anymore; they're scum." He revealed that US forces had struck Kharg Island — Iran's primary crude export hub — the previous night, and threatened further escalation: "Maybe we'll take over Kharg Island, and we may take over Kharg Island, and there's not a thing they can do about it." Those words hit the oil tape like a detonation. Brent surged more than 5% on Wednesday as traders priced the scenario that US military forces might seize or permanently neutralize the island that handles approximately 90% of Iran's crude oil exports — roughly 950 million barrels annually — and through which China, India, and South Korea receive the bulk of their Iranian crude. US CENTCOM separately confirmed it had struck approximately 90 Iranian military targets in the July 8 operation, including air defense systems, coastal surveillance assets, missile and drone storage sites, and IRGC naval capabilities along Iran's coastline. It was the second consecutive day of US strikes on Iran following CENTCOM's initial operation on July 7 in response to the Hormuz tanker attacks on three commercial vessels.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded by striking 85 US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait, and Iranian leadership accused Washington of violating the Islamabad MOU's core provisions. The IRGC issued a warning that it would "retaliate in a harsher way" in the coming days — a statement that markets are pricing as a near-certainty given the escalatory cycle now underway. Kharg Island's strategic significance cannot be overstated. Located approximately 55 kilometers off Iran's coast in the Persian Gulf, the island's deep-water terminals serve as the pipeline terminus for multiple Iranian offshore fields, and it handles essentially all of Iran's crude export volumes. During the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s, Iraqi bombing of Kharg was the primary lever used to throttle Iranian oil revenue. A US seizure in 2026 would be categorically more severe: it would represent a permanent, kinetic removal of Iran's ability to export crude — not a temporary disruption, but a structural elimination of 2.5–3 million barrels per day of supply from global markets. Brent's 5% surge on Wednesday reflected only the initial premium assigned to that scenario. If US forces moved from striking Kharg to occupying it, the tape would move another $15–20/bbl from current levels.

Amid the escalating military exchange, two data points arrived that complicate the supply narrative. The EIA's July 8 weekly petroleum report — covering the week ending July 3 — showed the first crude inventory build in weeks: +2.998 million barrels, against a forecast decline of 1.9 million barrels. Stocks stand at 411.4 million barrels, 6% below the five-year seasonal average. The build confirms that Gulf crude was reaching US shores even before the re-escalation — meaning the supply pipeline was normalizing precisely when the political architecture collapsed. That data has been almost entirely displaced by the geopolitical shock. Separately, natural gas diverged sharply from crude: Henry Hub front-month futures dropped more than 6% Thursday to a six-week low of approximately $3.01, held near $2.99 Friday — a move driven by two supply-specific factors entirely unrelated to the Iranian crisis. Freeport LNG, one of the largest US liquefied natural gas export facilities, began maintenance on pre-treatment and liquefaction facilities today, July 10, continuing through late August, sharply reducing feedgas demand. A 61 Bcf natural gas storage injection for the week ending July 3 far exceeded the 49 Bcf consensus forecast, widening the inventory surplus. The oil-gas divergence tells a layered story: crude markets are pricing Iranian geopolitical risk while gas markets are pricing domestic supply-demand fundamentals. That divergence will close only when the Iranian situation resolves — in one direction or the other.

news.headline: Trump Declares Ceasefire "Over" From NATO Ankara Summit — "I Don't Want to Deal With Them Anymore; They're Scum"
news.body: President Trump declared the US-Iran ceasefire "over" on July 8 from the NATO summit in Ankara, approximately three weeks after the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was signed on June 17. "I think it's over," Trump told reporters. "I don't want to deal with them anymore; they're scum." He said the US had struck Kharg Island the previous night and threatened additional military action, including a potential naval blockade reinstatement and seizure of Kharg Island. In a significant contradiction, Trump simultaneously allowed US negotiators to continue back-channel diplomatic discussions — a paradox the market is now pricing as either a maximum-pressure strategy or policy incoherence, with very different oil-price implications depending on which interpretation is correct.

news.headline: US Strikes Kharg Island — Trump Threatens Seizure of the Hub Handling 90% of Iran's Crude Exports; Oil Surges 5%+
news.body: US forces struck Kharg Island on the night of July 7-8 as part of CENTCOM's ~90-target operation against Iranian military assets. Trump revealed the strike and threatened outright seizure: "Maybe we'll take over Kharg Island, and we may take over Kharg Island, and there's not a thing they can do about it." Located 55 km off Iran's Persian Gulf coast, Kharg Island handles approximately 90% of Iran's crude oil exports (~950 million barrels annually), with China as the primary destination. During the Iran-Iraq War, Iraqi bombing of Kharg was the primary mechanism for throttling Iranian oil revenue; a US seizure in 2026 would structurally eliminate Iran's ability to export crude — removing an estimated 2.5–3 mb/d from global supply. Brent crude jumped more than 5% on Wednesday as traders assigned initial probability to the seizure scenario.

news.headline: Iran Retaliates: IRGC Strikes 85 US Military Sites in Bahrain and Kuwait — Threatens "Harsher Retaliation" in Coming Days
news.body: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps responded to the US strikes by targeting 85 US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait, and separately launched eight missiles at a US military base in Jordan (intercepted by Jordanian air defenses). Iranian leadership formally accused Washington of violating the Islamabad MOU. The IRGC issued a statement warning it would "retaliate in a harsher way" in the coming days. Iran's hard-line position frames the US strikes as treaty violations rather than legitimate responses to the July 7 tanker attacks — a framing that, if sustained, closes the diplomatic off-ramp and forces the market to price an extended military conflict rather than a resolvable crisis. The next 72 hours of Iranian escalation or de-escalation signaling are the decisive near-term variable for Brent's direction.

news.headline: First Crude Build in Weeks — EIA Reports +3.0M bbl for Week Ending July 3; Stocks 411.4M bbl, 6% Below 5-Yr Avg
news.body: The EIA's July 8 weekly petroleum status report delivered the first crude inventory build in multiple consecutive weeks: +2.998 million barrels for the week ending July 3, against a consensus forecast decline of 1.9 million barrels. Commercial crude stocks now stand at 411.4 million barrels, 6% below the five-year seasonal average. The build confirms that Gulf crude from restarted Iranian and Saudi fields was reaching US shores before the July 7-8 escalation — meaning the bearish supply-normalization thesis was materializing in the data precisely as the political framework collapsed. The July 15 EIA report will be the first inventory data capturing the period of re-escalation: whether tanker operators have re-routed or paused Hormuz transits will appear in the crude stock change.

news.headline: Henry Hub Hits Six-Week Low — Freeport LNG Maintenance Begins Today Through Late August; 61 Bcf Storage Build Exceeds Forecast
news.body: US natural gas front-month futures fell more than 6% Thursday to their lowest close since May 27, driven by two Iran-unrelated supply factors. Freeport LNG — one of the largest US LNG export facilities — began scheduled maintenance on pre-treatment and liquefaction facilities today, July 10, continuing through late August, sharply reducing feedgas demand. Separately, energy companies injected 61 billion cubic feet of gas into storage for the week ending July 3, exceeding the 49 Bcf consensus forecast and widening the inventory surplus over the five-year average. Henry Hub holds near $2.99 on Friday after Thursday's decline. The oil-gas divergence — crude holding near $77 while gas retreats toward $3 — reflects structurally different supply-demand dynamics: crude priced on Iranian geopolitics, gas priced on domestic infrastructure and storage fundamentals.

news.headline: US Forces Complete Second Round of Iran Strikes — ~90 Targets Hit Including Air Defense, IRGC Boats, Coastal Surveillance; Kharg Island Struck
news.body: CENTCOM confirmed that US forces struck approximately 90 Iranian military targets on July 8, including more than 60 IRGC boats, air defense systems, coastal surveillance assets, missile and drone storage sites, and military logistics infrastructure along Iran's coastline — the second consecutive day of operations following the initial July 7 response to the Hormuz tanker attacks. CENTCOM said the operations were intended to impose costs on Iran for violating the ceasefire and to degrade Iran's ability to attack commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Trump's confirmation that Kharg Island was among the targets struck elevated the market-moving significance of the operations far beyond a standard counter-IRGC campaign: Kharg Island's destruction or seizure crosses the threshold from tactical pressure to strategic supply shock.

events.name: Kharg Island: Will the US Seize It? The Single Largest Supply-Shock Risk on the 2026 Calendar
events.impact: Trump's Kharg Island seizure threat is the most consequential supply-risk statement made since the war began on February 28. Kharg handles ~90% of Iran's crude exports (~950 million barrels annually). A strike that damages throughput capacity is already partially priced. A full seizure or destruction of loading infrastructure would structurally eliminate 2.5–3 mb/d of Iranian crude from global supply — a loss that OPEC+ cannot compensate for with its current spare capacity buffer of approximately 2.5 mb/d. This scenario carries a price impact larger than any single event on the 2026 calendar. The three probable outcomes: (1) US maintains strike pressure but does not physically seize Kharg — surgical degradation, some throughput reduction, ceasefire preserved in modified form; (2) US occupies Kharg temporarily as a maximum-pressure bargaining chip — Iranian exports halted for weeks, Brent $85–92; (3) Permanent US control or destruction of Kharg export infrastructure — 2.5–3 mb/d removed from supply; Brent targets $95–$105.
events.market_impact: No Kharg seizure (outcome 1): $2–3/bbl giveback from current levels as market de-risks; Brent tests $73–$75. Temporary occupation (outcome 2): $8–15/bbl immediate spike; Brent $85–$92; WTI above $82. Permanent seizure/destruction (outcome 3): $18–28/bbl; Brent $95–$105; worst-case Hormuz re-closure adds further premium.

events.name: Iran's "Harsher Retaliation" Warning — IRGC Escalation or De-Escalation: The Second-Order Variable
events.impact: The IRGC's explicit warning of "harsher retaliation in coming days" must be evaluated against two competing Iranian imperatives: the hardliners' institutional incentive to retaliate kinetically, and the Iranian government's economic imperative to preserve the residual export infrastructure at Kharg and keep some diplomatic path to crude revenue. Iran's 85-site retaliation in Bahrain and Kuwait was calibrated to stay below a threshold of direct US casualties — the line that historically triggers full US escalation. A harder retaliation targeting US naval assets, carrier groups, or bases in Iraq and Syria would cross that threshold. Critically, if Iranian missiles or drones directly damage Kharg's own loading infrastructure in a retaliatory miscalculation, the export disruption becomes Iranian self-inflicted — a bizarre but historically documented risk in Iran-Iraq War precedents.
events.market_impact: Calibrated retaliation (Bahrain/Kuwait-style): $1–2/bbl additional premium; Brent holds $76–$78. Escalation to US naval assets or Iraqi bases: $4–6/bbl spike; Brent targets $80–$83. Iranian strike on Kharg or Hormuz shipping lanes: $10–18/bbl; catastrophic tail-risk scenario.

events.name: Diplomatic Back-Channel: Is the Ceasefire Truly "Over" or Is This a Maximum-Pressure Gambit?
events.impact: Trump's most consequential self-contradiction was declaring the ceasefire "over" while simultaneously allowing US negotiators to continue diplomatic discussions with Iranian counterparts. This paradox is the hinge point of the entire market range. If the ceasefire declaration was a maximum-pressure tactic — designed to force Iran to disavow the IRGC attacks and return to the Islamabad framework on more favorable terms — then diplomatic channels remain live and the ceasefire can be restored within 48–72 hours of credible Iranian concessions. If the ceasefire declaration reflects a genuine policy shift toward regime-pressure or military resolution, the Islamabad MOU is dead and the market must price a sustained, open-ended conflict. The difference between these two interpretations is approximately $10–15/bbl in either direction from the current $76.57 Brent.
events.market_impact: Ceasefire restored via back-channel (pressure gambit): $4–6/bbl relief; Brent tests $70–$73; bear fundamentals reassert. Ceasefire genuinely abandoned: $8–12/bbl additional premium; Brent targets $82–$88. Kharg seizure proceeds: compound with outcome from event 1 above.

events.name: EIA Weekly Petroleum Report — First Post-Escalation Inventory Data; Will Hormuz Disruption Show in US Crude Stocks?
events.impact: The EIA's July 15 report will cover the week ending July 10 — the first inventory period capturing the full re-escalation. The July 8 report showed the first crude build in weeks (+3.0M bbl), confirming Gulf crude was arriving before the ceasefire collapse. The July 15 data will answer whether tanker operators paused or re-routed Hormuz transits in the days following the July 7-8 attacks. A draw after the first build would suggest incoming supply disruption. A second consecutive build would confirm supply was already fully normalized before the political collapse — adding a bearish data counterpoint to the geopolitical premium.
events.market_impact: Second consecutive build (2–5M bbl): limited price impact; bearish data note in geopolitically dominated tape. First draw in two weeks (−1 to −3M bbl): $0.50–1/bbl supportive; confirms Hormuz supply disruption materializing. Large draw (>3M bbl): $1.50–2.50/bbl supportive; confirms significant transit disruption; adds fundamental weight to geopolitical premium.

events.name: Sixth OPEC+ Hike or Emergency Pause? War Re-Escalation Upends Market-Share Calculus
events.impact: Before the ceasefire collapse, the September OPEC+ ministerial was the first opportunity for Riyadh to pause the five-month hike cycle without losing face — Brent at $71.89 had been pressing against the Saudi fiscal breakeven. The Kharg Island threat and ceasefire collapse fundamentally alter that calculation. If US forces seize Kharg and Iranian exports are curtailed, global supply tightens sharply and Riyadh's market-share strategy becomes less necessary — Saudi Arabia gets fiscal support from geopolitically elevated prices without taking a production cut. OPEC+'s five consecutive hikes assumed Iranian supply was flowing freely through Hormuz; that assumption is no longer valid. The sixth hike for September is now contingent on the conflict's trajectory.
events.market_impact: Conflict persists, sixth hike shelved: supply tightening on both Iranian and OPEC+ fronts; Brent supported at $78–$82 through year-end. Rapid ceasefire restoration, sixth hike proceeds: bearish; Brent risks mid-$60s by Q4 2026. Emergency OPEC+ cuts to defend prices: unlikely but would signal crisis-level fiscal pressure; prices $85+.

paragraphs: Three weeks ago, the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding was the most bullish-for-peace event in the oil market since February 28. This column tracked the sequential de-risking: Brent fell from $144 in April to $71.89 by July 7, with five consecutive OPEC+ hikes, Saudi Arabia's record OSP cuts, and the IEA's surplus forecast all pointing toward a structural bear case. On July 5 I wrote: "The August 21 waiver expiry is priced at zero risk; any event that raises that probability produces a $5–8/bbl shock from a tape with no cushion." Two days later the Hormuz tanker attacks arrived. Two days after that, Trump declared the ceasefire "over," US forces struck Kharg Island, and the president threatened to seize the hub through which 90% of Iran's crude exports flow. Brent has moved from $73.29 (Wednesday's briefing) to $76.57 today — a 4.5% gain over two sessions. That is the opening adjustment in a market that is trying, and largely failing, to price three wildly different outcomes from a single set of facts.

My read on the current situation: The ceasefire is not simply "stressed" — it is functionally suspended. But it is not definitively dead, and the distinction matters enormously for where Brent trades next week. Trump's paradox — declaring the ceasefire "over" while allowing negotiators to continue talking — is either the most sophisticated maximum-pressure campaign of his presidency or genuine policy incoherence. If it is a pressure campaign, the Islamabad MOU can be restored within 48–72 hours of Iranian concessions, and Brent would give back $4–6 as bear fundamentals reassert. If it reflects a genuine shift toward Iranian regime pressure or military resolution, Brent has another $15–20 to move higher as Kharg Island seizure probability approaches certainty. The market is at $76.57 because it cannot distinguish between those two scenarios. It will be forced to do so within 72 hours as Iranian signals clarify.

What has structurally changed since the last briefing: Kharg Island is now a live military objective. That is categorically different from anything priced in the prior six weeks. Saudi Arabia's $11/bbl OSP cut and OPEC+'s five consecutive hikes were both predicated on Iranian crude flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz. A Kharg Island seizure removes the supply entirely — not by blocking the Strait, but by eliminating Iran's ability to load crude onto tankers regardless of whether the Strait is navigable. The EIA's first crude build (+3.0M bbl, week ending July 3) is almost irrelevant against this backdrop except as a baseline: it confirms supply was normalizing before the collapse, which means a rapid diplomatic resolution would see that normalization resume quickly. The natural gas divergence — six-week low on Freeport maintenance while crude holds near $77 — is the one clean domestic data signal: the commodity complex is not in a generalized risk-on move; it is pricing a specifically Iranian supply shock.

My call: Brent $74–$84 for the week, with the range driven entirely by Kharg Island's fate and the diplomatic back-channel's viability. Rapid ceasefire restoration via pressure gambit: $70–$73, bear trend reasserts, OPEC+ hike cycle resumes, Brent tests the low $70s. Kharg Island degraded but not seized, sustained military pressure: $76–$80, geopolitical premium holds at current levels. Kharg Island seized or Iranian supply structurally disrupted: $84–$92, six-week rally, worst-case $90+ if Hormuz access threatened concurrently. Friday's $76.57 is the maximum-uncertainty price. It will not hold — resolution, in either direction, is imminent and violent. The only position that makes sense at this price is one where you know which outcome you're betting on.
